title: Superconductivity, pseudogap and marginal Fermi liquid in a relative-momentum-local theory
abstract: Cuprate superconductors host \(d\)-wave superconductivity (SC), a pseudogap (PG) with Fermi arcs and a strange metal (SM) with incoherent excitations and temperature-linear resistivity. These regimes emerge from the same doped Mott system but are usually described separately. Here a relative-momentum-local (RML) theory is constructed, with the exact spin-singlet Cooper representation of antiferromagnetic superexchange in the \(t\)-\(J\) model serving as a common thread. Pair correlations organize the low-energy behaviour of this Cooper channel into phase-coherent static SC, phase-incoherent quasi-static PG and phase-incoherent dynamic SM. A static RML prescription yields an exactly solvable PG Hamiltonian with nodal electron poles, antinodal gaps, resolution-broadened Fermi arcs and gapless charge-\(2e\) Cooper surfaces. A Cooper-surface Lifshitz transition generates logarithmic enhancements in the specific-heat coefficient and charge response without a spin singularity. The particle-particle continuum at finite centre-of-mass momentum produces Ohmic damping, while a dynamic RML prescription yields a one-loop self-energy with marginal-Fermi-liquid scaling. Spectral-weight transfer in the physical pair spectrum diagnoses the PG--SM crossover, whereas nonzero phase stiffness and global phase coherence identify SC. The RML theory relates single-particle, pair-sensitive and thermodynamic probes to three infrared organizations of one Cooper channel. A decisive experimental signature would be zero-energy Cooper-surface ridges in two-electron angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (2e-ARPES).
summary: This paper introduces a Relative-Momentum-Local (RML) theory to unify the description of superconductivity, pseudogap, and strange metal states in cuprates. It achieves this by analyzing how pair correlation functions organize into distinct static, quasi-static, or dynamic behaviors depending on the electronic phase. The work provides concrete diagnostic tools, such as spectral weight transfer and zero-energy ARPES features, to distinguish these correlated quantum phases.
main_problem: The paper addresses how three distinct low-energy regimes—Superconductivity (SC), Pseudogap (PG), and Strange Metal (SM)—emerge from the same doped Mott system in cuprate superconductors.
main_result: A Relative-Momentum-Local (RML) theory unifies these descriptions by analyzing the infrared organization of a single Cooper channel, linking SC to phase coherence, PG to quasi-static correlations, and SM to dynamic damping.
method: The authors construct an RML theory based on the $t$-$J$ model, using pair correlation functions ($P_{qq'}, C_{\alpha\alpha'}$) and spectral analysis to diagnose the crossover between regimes.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a doped Mott insulator governed by the $t$-$J$ Hamiltonian. The theory uses an RML approach that treats single-particle, pair-sensitive, and thermodynamic probes through various correlation functions.
key_observables: Phase stiffness (zero for PG/SM, non-zero for SC), spectral weight transfer in the pair spectrum ($A_{	ext{pair}}$), and zero-energy Cooper-surface ridges detectable by $2e$-ARPES.
important_parameters: Doping level, temperature relative to characteristic scales ($T^*$, $T_{BKT}$), and momentum/frequency variables ($\mathbf{Q}, \Omega$).
main_assumptions: The theory relies on the Gutzwiller approximation for the no-double-occupancy constraint. The derivation of RML prescriptions from a common dressed Cooper kernel is noted as an open problem.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates how pair correlators ($P_{qq'}$ and $C_{\alpha\alpha'}$) distinguish the three regimes: PG shows enhanced block-diagonal autocorrelation, while SM involves broad spectral functions over finite momenta.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by noting the coexistence of SC, PG, and SM. It then develops the RML theory using pair correlation functions to map out distinct behaviors for each regime (static/quasi-static/dynamic). Finally, it discusses crossover mechanisms (PG-SM via spectral weight transfer; PG-SC/SM-SC via phase coherence restoration) and proposes key experimental signatures.
why_interesting: The unified theoretical framework connecting single-particle, pair, and thermodynamic responses across multiple correlated phases is highly relevant for understanding complex many-body dynamics in strongly interacting quantum materials.
